pages.text:
*The Bearer's Almanac, Entry 18: Even a villain has a reason, and the reason is usually fear.*

The warehouse held the heavy, biting scent of wet hemp and old tar, a smell that seemed to coat the back of the throat. Outside, rain drummed a frantic rhythm on the thatched roof, a relentless percussion that vibrated in Wen’s teeth and offered no true shelter from the cold seeping through the planks. She sat on a stack of coiled ropes, knees drawn up to her chest, watching her breath fog in the dim air. The white streak in her hair caught the faint glow of the oil lamp, a stark, unnatural line against the black.

Auntie Mo sat cross-legged on the floor, her conical hat removed so that her grey hair lay loose and tangled around her shoulders. Stripped of her ferry pole and her usual authority, she looked smaller, and her hands, usually steady as stone, trembled slightly as she pried open a leather case wedged behind a false panel in the raft’s keel.

"Who sent these?" Shen Yu asked. He stood by the window, his back to them, watching the rain slash against the dark water of the harbor. His voice was tight, controlled, the voice of a man holding a secret together by force of will. "The ink is fresh. The seals are broken."

Mo did not answer immediately. She lifted a bundle of parchment from the case, the paper thick and expensive, feeling like skin under the fingers. She spread them out on the wooden floor, smoothing them with careful, deliberate motions.

Wen leaned forward. The dates on the letters were stamped in red ink, but the oldest one, tucked beneath the others, bore a mark that made her stomach drop. Eleven years.

"Eleven years ago," Wen whispered. "Mother was alive."

Mo’s hand hovered over the parchment. "These are addressed to her," the ferrywoman said, her voice low and rough. "From the man who stopped the river."

Shen Yu turned around, his glasses fogged by the sudden change in temperature. "Lord Bao Heng," he said. "I have seen his seal. I did not think he wrote letters. I thought he sent orders."

"He does both," Mo said. "And he writes to your mother, Wen Lan. Not to the Bearer. To Lin Hua."

Wen reached for the top letter. Her fingers brushed the paper, and a shiver ran up her arm that had nothing to do with the cold. She looked at Mo, then at Shen Yu. The rain hammered harder, drowning out the sound of the river, leaving only the ticking of the water in the gutters and the beating of her own heart.

"I am not your mother," Wen said.

"No," Mo agreed. "But he thinks you are. And he is afraid of what you might do."

Wen picked up the letter. The leather case was heavy, full of more. She looked at the pile, a stack of silence that had been kept for over a decade.

pages.text:
The first letter was dated the same month the river had stopped, but the tone was not one of command. It was weary. It was the voice of a man who had been keeping a vigil for a long time and was tired of the watch.

*Lin Hua,*

*You will have heard the rumors. You know what is happening to the glaciers. I have sent surveyors to the high peaks. The ice is retreating. The wetlands that feed the headwaters are shrinking. In twenty years, perhaps less, the Clear River will not be enough. The drought will come, and it will not be a temporary sleep. It will be a death.*

*We have a hundred thousand people downstream. Farmers, fishers, children. If the water stops, they die. I have no choice. I must store what I can now, for the day when there is nothing left to save. It is a terrible burden, but it is the only one I am willing to carry.*

*You left. You went to the Source and you did not come back. I understand your fear, but fear is not wisdom. Fear is a wall. I am building a dam. I am building a future.*

*Join me. Your knowledge of the river, your understanding of the flow, would be invaluable. We can work together to manage the scarcity. We can save them all.*

*If you do not come, I will continue alone. I will not let them starve.*

*Your friend, Bao Heng.*

Wen read the letter twice. The words were not cruel. They were logical. They were the kind of words a sensible person would use when the world was ending and they had no other plan.

"He is not a monster," Shen Yu said. He had moved to stand beside Wen, his face pale in the lamplight. "I reported on him. I watched him. He sleeps four hours a night. He eats last. He visits the orphanages in the capital. He is not evil, Wen. He is just... certain."

"Certainty is dangerous," Mo said from the corner. She was cleaning her nails with a knife, a sharp, rhythmic scraping sound that cut through the silence. "A man who is certain he is right does not ask questions. He does not listen. He builds walls."

"He is saving people," Wen said. Her voice sounded strange to her own ears, hollow and thin. "He says the glaciers are shrinking. He says the drought is coming. If he is right..."

"Then he is stealing from the living to feed the dead," Mo interrupted. "That is not saving. That is hoarding."

Wen looked back at the letter. *I will not let them starve.* It was a promise. It was a threat. And it was signed with a name she had heard in whispers, in the market stalls and the ferry docks, a name that meant power and silence and the heavy, unyielding weight of a seal.

pages.text:
There was only one reply in the case, tucked into the bottom of the leather sleeve where the light did not reach. It was not a letter but a single sheet of paper, folded into a small square. The handwriting was different from the Lord’s, smaller and sharper, written in a blue ink that had faded to the pale grey of river mist.

*You are storing water for a drought you are causing.*

*You believe that because you take it, it is yours. You believe that because you hold it, it is safe. But a river is not a bank, Bao Heng. You cannot deposit the future and withdraw it when you are afraid. You cannot own the flow. You can only manage the channel.*

*Take only what you will give back. That is the law of the water. That is the law of the land. If you take more than you return, you do not save the people. You kill them. You kill the river.*

*I am going to the Source to see for myself. I will not watch you break the world to save it. I will not be part of your fear.*

*Tell the people the truth. Tell them the river is not gone. It is waiting. And if you keep waiting, it will never come.*

*Lin Hua.*

Wen stared at the words, feeling the chill of the ink seep into her own skin. *Take only what you will give back.* It was the first rule she had learned, the one she had broken at Hollow Pool, the one that had cost her the warmth in her hands.

"She knew," Shen Yu said, his voice barely a whisper in the quiet room. "She knew what he was doing. She tried to stop him."

"She went to the Source," Wen said, her gaze fixed on the signature. "She went to see the ice."

"And she never came down," Mo said. It was not a question, but the silence that followed was heavy with the sound of unsaid words.

Wen looked at the white streak in her hair, which had grown longer over the weeks, creeping up her scalp with a cold and persistent tenacity that she had tried to hide under her hat and scarf.

"She did not stay away because she was afraid," Wen said, her voice steady despite the tremor in her hands. "She stayed because she gave too much, I think. She tried to hold the river alone, and it took her."

Mo looked at her, the ferrywoman’s eyes hard and bright with a grief she had not yet learned to name. "You are making the same mistake. You are thinking that if you hold the water, you can save them. You are thinking that your power is a dam."

"It is not," Wen said. "It is a channel."

"Then open it," Mo said. "Let it flow. Let it go. That is the only way to keep it."

Wen looked again at the letter from her mother. The ink was faded, almost invisible, but the words remained clear and unyielding against the paper. *Tell the people the truth.*

pages.text:
Shen Yu had his map case open on the floor. He had been drawing, sketching lines and numbers, trying to make sense of the data he had collected over the last few years. Now, he pulled out a sheet of paper covered in dense, intricate calculations.

"I have the reports from the high peaks," he said. "From the surveyors who work for the Guild. They are not lying about the ice. The glacier at the Source has shrunk by a third in a generation. The wetlands are drying up. The water table is dropping."

He looked up, his glasses catching the light. "The Lord is not lying about the danger. The drought is coming. The water is going. That is a fact."

Wen felt a cold knot in her stomach. "But he is wrong about the answer," she said. "Storing it is not the answer."

"No," Shen Yu agreed. "He thinks that if he holds it, he can control it. He thinks that if he takes it from the river, he can distribute it fairly. But he is not distributing it. He is selling it. He is using the scarcity to build a power structure. He is turning the river into a weapon."

"He is afraid," Wen said.

"He is afraid of losing control," Shen Yu corrected. "Fear makes men hoard. It makes them build walls. It makes them believe that if they take enough, they will be safe."

Wen looked at Mo. The ferrywoman was watching them, her face unreadable. She had heard this argument before. She had heard it in the villages, in the markets, in the quiet corners of the world where people whispered about the missing water.

"A frightened man stores water," Mo said. "A wise man shares it."

"Sharing is not always easy," Shen Yu said. "Sharing is not always fair. Sometimes, the only way to share is to take."

"No," Mo said. "Taking is not sharing. Taking is stealing. Sharing is giving. And giving is not the same as keeping."

Wen looked at the letters again. Her mother’s words swirled in her mind. *Take only what you will give back.*

"I agree with half of what he says," Wen said. "The water is going. That is true. But the other half is a lie. He is not saving us. He is trapping us."

"Then what do we do?" Shen Yu asked. "We cannot just walk away. The people are thirsty. The farmers are dying."

"We walk to the Source," Wen said. "We find the water. We open the gates."

"The gates are locked," Mo said. "The Lord has them. He has the keys."

"Then we break them," Wen said.

Mo looked at her. "It is not that simple, child. The gates are not just wood and iron. They are stone. They are the mountain. You cannot break the mountain."

Wen looked at her hands. The frost on her fingertips was gone, but the cold remained, a deep, aching chill that seemed to have settled into her bones.

"I am not breaking the mountain," Wen said. "I am opening the channel."

pages.text:
The sound of footsteps on the deck above was heavy. It was not the light, shuffling step of a rat, or the soft, hesitant tread of a thief, but the solid, rhythmic thud of boots on wood.

Wen, Mo, and Shen Yu froze. The oil lamp between them flickered, casting long, jittery shadows across the walls.

"Who is there?" Mo called out. Her voice was steady, but her hand had moved to the small knife in her pocket.

A voice answered from above. It was young, sharp, and authoritative. "By order of the Merchant Guild, surrender the bearer and the surveyor. The warehouse is surrounded."

Shen Yu’s face went white. "They have the seal," he whispered. "They know exactly where we are."

Mo looked at Wen. "We have to go through the water," she said. "The harbor is dark. The current is strong. If we can reach the outer rafts, we can lose them."

"The water is cold," Wen said. "And my power..."

"Your power is not the problem," Mo said. "The problem is that you are afraid to use it. You are afraid of the cost."

Wen looked at the white streak in her hair. It was longer now, reaching down to her shoulder. It pulsed with a faint, cold light.

"I am not afraid of the cost," Wen said. "I am afraid of what I will become."

Mo grabbed her hand. Her grip was firm, warm, and real. "Then do not think about what you will become," she said. "Think about who you are. You are the Bearer. And the Bearer does not hoard. The Bearer flows."

The footsteps stopped. The door to the warehouse creaked open.

Light flooded in, blinding and harsh.

"Out," a soldier shouted. "Now."

Wen did not hesitate. She pulled Shen Yu up, grabbed Mo’s hand, and sprinted toward the small, unmarked hatch in the floor.
